records.title: Patient-reported outcome measures after multifocal and extended depth of focus intraocular lens implantation in refractive lens exchange and cataract surgery.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Patient-reported outcome measures after multifocal and extended depth of focus intraocular lens implantation in refractive lens exchange and cataract surgery.
content.abstract: Presbyopia-correcting intraocular lenses (IOLs) represent a fast-growing segment of ophthalmic surgery. The evaluation of lens performance has undergone a fundamental shift: best-corrected visual acuity alone is an insufficient measure of the clinical benefit of premium IOLs, whose true value lies in spectacle independence, visual quality, and visual function in daily activities. In that regard, patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are a cornerstone of presbyopia-correcting IOL assessment. This review provides an overview of the current landscape of IOLs, PROM instruments and their limitations, visual function outcomes across IOL types and comorbidities, and future directions. Higher near performance often comes at the cost of greater dysphotopsia, and no single IOL design dominates across all PROM domains. Optimal IOL selection or combination therefore requires identifying which PROM domain matters most to the individual patient. While not absolute contraindications, dry eye disease and prior refractive surgery are the strongest predictors of suboptimal outcomes and therefore warrant careful preoperative consideration. As visual demands increasingly shift toward near and intermediate distances with growing digital device use, clinicians and manufacturers must align IOL design priorities and patient selection with evolving patient needs. The visual function index (VF)-14 questionnaire and most other vision-specific PROM instruments were developed in a pre-digital era and require modernization to remain valid measures of patient success. In an aging active population, multifocal and extended depth of focus IOLs, when matched to the right patients, represent one of surgery's most impactful quality-of-life interventions.

records.title: Combined Accelerated Crosslinking With Laser In Situ Keratomileusis (LASIK) for Myopic Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Combined Accelerated Crosslinking With Laser In Situ Keratomileusis (LASIK) for Myopic Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To compare laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) and Simultaneous LASIK and accelerated Crosslinking (LASIK Xtra) for myopia correction.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Methods

A search of PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and China National Knowledge Internet was conducted up to October 1, 2024 to identify studies comparing LASIK and LASIK Xtra for myopia correction. The outcome of visual acuity and refraction, safety, efficiency, predictability, stability, postoperative corneal thickness and endothelial cell count were measure.

Results

A total of 1,647 eyes (836 LASIK, 811 LASIK Xtra) from 15 studies were included. LASIK demonstrated superior postoperative uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA) compared to LASIK Xtra, with a mean difference (MD) of -0.03 (8 studies, n = 750 eyes; 95% CI: -0.04 to -0.01, P = .007) at 1 month and (7 studies, n = 672 eyes; MD= -0.01 95% CI: -0.02 to 0.00, P = .02) for long-term results (≥6 months). No significant differences were found in corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA; 6 studies, n = 530 eyes; MD = 0.00, 95% CI: -0.01, 0.00, P = .32), spherical equivalent (14 studies, n = 1639 eyes; MD = 0.03, 95% CI: -0.03, 0.08; P = .40), safety (8 studies, n = 779 eyes; odds ratios [OR]= 0.70; 95% CI: 0.39, 1.26; P = .23), efficiency (11 studies, n = 921 eyes; OR = 0.75, 95% CI: 0.54, 1.05, P = .10), predictability (11 studies, n = 971 eyes; OR= 1.03, 95% CI: 0.72, 1.47, P = .86), stability (3 studies, n = 90 eyes; OR = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.21, 2.28, P = .55). Subgroup analysis indicated a higher risk of postoperative CDVA loss in the Ectasia Risk Group undergoing LASIK-Xtra (OR= 0.20, 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.97, P = .05). The 30 mW/cm² for 90 seconds (2.7 J/cm²) irradiation protocol in LASIK Xtra may resulted in worse UDVA compared to LASIK (MD= -0.01, 95% CI: -0.03 to -0.001, P = .05). The certainty of evidence for the outcomes ranged from "low to very low".

Conclusions

Current evidence suggests that LASIK offers a statistically significant advantage in UDVA compared to LASIK Xtra, especially when LASIK Xtra irradiation protocol of 30 mW/cm² for 90 seconds (2.7 J/cm²) is applied. However, given the low to very low certainty of evidence, these findings require cautious interpretation and further confirmation through long-term studies.

records.title: Cytopathology and Prognostic Accuracy of 15-GEP/PRAME: The Collaborative Ocular Oncology Group Study 2.

content.title: Cytopathology and Prognostic Accuracy of 15-GEP/PRAME: The Collaborative Ocular Oncology Group Study 2.
content.abstract:
Importance

Gene expression profiling (GEP) reliably predicts metastatic uveal melanoma risk and is used to manage uveal melanoma (UM) in patients with this diagnosis. Efforts to refine molecular prognostication continue.

Objective

To determine if confirmatory cytopathology findings influence the prognostic accuracy of a commercially available GEP/Preferentially Expressed Antigen in Melanoma (PRAME) assay.

Design, setting, and participants

The Collaborative Ocular Oncology Group 2 study, a prospective cohort study, was conducted from 2017 to 2020 with follow-up recorded at 6-month intervals. This was a multicenter study that included patients with choroidal and/or ciliary body melanoma and results from a 15-GEP and PRAME RNA expression (15-GEP/PRAME) assay. Patients with iris tumors or less than 6 months' follow-up were excluded. Study data were analyzed from April 2025 to July 2026.

Exposures

15-GEP/PRAME, cytopathology, and next-generation sequencing (NGS).

Main outcomes and measures

Metastatic uveal melanoma rates in patients who had 15-GEP/PRAME and confirmatory cytopathology (CCP) results confirming or suspicious for UM (GEP+CCP) were compared with those who had 15-GEP/PRAME and no cytopathology performed, or unknown or nondiagnostic cytopathology results (GEP only). UM-associated variants identified by NGS were also evaluated.

Results

Of 1537 patients (mean [SD] age, 62.0 [13.4] years; 787 male [51.2%]), 727 (47.3%) had CCP results, and 810 (52.7%) had nondiagnostic cytopathology results or no cytopathology performed. Class 2/PRAME+ tumors were more common (136 of 727 [18.7%]) in the GEP+CCP group than in the GEP-only group (72 of 810 [8.9%]; 9.8% difference; 95% CI, 6.4-13.3; P <.001), whereas class 1/PRAME- tumors were less common (330 of 727 [45.4%] vs 495 of 810 [61.1%]; 15.7% difference; 95% CI, 10.8-20.6; P <.001). In patients with GEP+CCP, 22.7% (n = 165) developed metastasis vs 15.4% (n = 125) in patients with GEP only (7.3% difference, 95% CI, 3.3-11.2; P < .001). Adjusting for 15-GEP/PRAME status, there were no differences in metastasis rates between CCP groups. Of 1327 patients with successful NGS, 94.1% (605 of 643) in the GEP+CCP group and 71.9% (492 of 684) in the GEP-only group had a UM-associated variant (22.2% difference, 95% CI, 18.3-26.0; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance

Results of this cohort study reveal that no differences in metastasis outcomes were observed between patients with and without CCP within any GEP/PRAME categories. UM-associated variants were found less frequently in the GEP-only group than in the GEP+CCP group. In this cohort, 15-GEP/PRAME classification without CCP retained prognostic validity, supporting its clinical consideration in guiding metastatic surveillance in cases in which cytopathology is unavailable.

records.title: STRUCTURE-FUNCTION ASSOCIATION BETWEEN CONTRAST SENSITIVITY FUNCTION AND OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY FEATURES IN PATIENTS WITH IDIOPATHIC EPIRETINAL MEMBRANE.

content.title: STRUCTURE-FUNCTION ASSOCIATION BETWEEN CONTRAST SENSITIVITY FUNCTION AND OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY FEATURES IN PATIENTS WITH IDIOPATHIC EPIRETINAL MEMBRANE.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Investigate the structure-function relationships between epiretinal membrane (ERM) stage, tractional abnormalities, and the gap area between the ERM and the retinal surface, in relation to visual acuity and quantitative contrast sensitivity function in patients with idiopathic epiretinal membrane.

Methods

This was a retrospective, cross-sectional study involving 111 participants diagnosed with idiopathic ERM. All patients underwent a comprehensive ophthalmologic examination, spectral-domain optical coherence tomography imaging using the SPECTRALIS Heidelberg system, and contrast sensitivity (CS) testing using the quantitative contrast sensitivity function method.

Results

Progressive stages of ERM were associated with declines in both CS and visual acuity (β* = -0.45 to -0.19, P < 0.02), with CS showing a more pronounced reduction than visual acuity, especially between controls and Stage 1. Ectopic inner foveal layer thickness exhibited a similar pattern of decline in both visual acuity (β* = 0.42, P < 0.001) and CS (β* = -0.46 to -0.18, all P < 0.02). By contrast, SUKIMA showed no significant association with any of the visual measurements assessed. Among the tractional abnormalities, the cotton ball sign correlated with diminished vision, particularly reflected by a notable drop in CS at the highest spatial frequencies tested with reduced CS at 12 cycles per degree (β* = -0.44, P = 0.02) and 18 cycles per degree (β* = -0.46, P = 0.02).

Conclusion

Quantitative contrast sensitivity function testing is particularly important for assessing visual function in ERM development, especially in the early stages.

records.title: Longitudinal Changes in Scleral Thickness after Half-dose Photodynamic Therapy in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy.

content.title: Longitudinal Changes in Scleral Thickness after Half-dose Photodynamic Therapy in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To evaluate longitudinal changes in scleral thickness after half-dose photodynamic therapy (PDT) in eyes with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) in parallel with widefield assessment of choroidal thickness.

Methods

This retrospective observational study included 41 eyes of 41 patients with unilateral CSC who underwent half-dose PDT for persistent subretinal fluid and completed 12 months of follow-up. Scleral thickness was measured in 4 quadrants using anterior-segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) at baseline and at 3 and 12 months after PDT. Widefield choroidal thickness was assessed using widefield swept-source OCT with an 18-mm grid divided into 9 sectors. Untreated fellow eyes served as a reference group.

Results

In treated eyes, widefield choroidal thickness decreased significantly at 3 months after PDT across all 9 predefined sectors (all P < 0.05) and remained reduced at 12 months, with no significant differences between 3 and 12 months. In untreated fellow eyes, no consistent longitudinal changes in choroidal thickness were observed; however, a statistically significant reduction was noted only in the outer superonasal sector at 3 months (P = 0.015). In contrast, scleral thickness showed no significant changes at any time point in either treated or fellow eyes (all P > 0.05).

Conclusions

Despite widespread and sustained choroidal thinning after half-dose PDT, scleral thickness remained unchanged for at least 12 months in eyes with CSC. These findings suggest that scleral thickening in CSC is unlikely to represent a readily reversible response to treatment-associated choroidal changes and may instead reflect a relatively stable anatomical feature.

records.title: Genome-Wide Association Study of Age-Related Macular Degeneration Reveals 2 New Loci Implying Shared Genetic Components with Central Serous Chorioretinopathy.

content.title: Genome-Wide Association Study of Age-Related Macular Degeneration Reveals 2 New Loci Implying Shared Genetic Components with Central Serous Chorioretinopathy.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To investigate the genetic architecture of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in a Japanese population.

Design

Genome-wide association study (GWAS).

Participants

Three thousand seven hundred seventy-two patients with AMD and 16 770 control participants from the Japanese population were enrolled in the association analyses.

Methods

We conducted a meta-analysis of 2 independent GWASs that included a total of 2663 patients with AMD and 9471 control participants using the imputation reference panel for genotype imputation specified for the Japanese population (n = 3541). A replication study was performed using an independent set of 1109 patients with AMD and 7299 control participants.

Main outcome measures

Associations of genetic variants with AMD.

Results

A meta-analysis of the 2 GWASs identified 6 loci significantly associated with AMD (P < 5.0 × 10-8). Of these loci, 4 were known to be associated with AMD (CFH, C2/FB, TNFRSF10A, and ARMS2), and 2 were novel (rs4147157 near WBP1L and rs76228488 near GATA5). The newly identified associations were confirmed in a replication study (P < 0.01). After the meta-analysis of all datasets, we observed strong associations in these loci (P = 1.88 × 10-12 and P = 1.35 × 10-9 for meta-analysis for rs4147157 and rs76228488, respectively). When we looked up the associations in the reported central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) GWAS conducted in the Japanese population, both loci were associated significantly with CSC (P = 4.86 × 10-3 and P = 4.28 × 10-3 for rs4147157 and rs76228488, respectively). We performed a genetic colocalization analysis for these loci and estimated that the posterior probabilities of shared causal variants between AMD and CSC were 0.39 and 0.60 for WBP1L and GATA5, respectively. Genetic correlation analysis focusing on the epidemiologically suggested clinical risk factors implicated shared polygenic architecture between AMD and smoking cessation (rg [the measure of genetic correlation] = -0.33; P = 0.01; false discovery rate, 0.099).

Conclusions

Our findings imply shared genetic components conferring the risk of both AMD and CSC.

Financial disclosure(s)

Proprietary or commercial disclosure may be found after the references.

records.title: Myocilin misfolding and glaucoma: A 20-year update.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Myocilin misfolding and glaucoma: A 20-year update.
content.abstract: Mutations in the gene MYOC account for approximately 5% of cases of primary open angle glaucoma (POAG). MYOC encodes for the protein myocilin, a multimeric secreted glycoprotein composed of N-terminal coiled-coil (CC) and leucine zipper (LZ) domains that are connected via a disordered linker to a 30 kDa olfactomedin (OLF) domain. More than 90% of glaucoma-causing mutations are localized to the OLF domain. While myocilin is expressed in numerous tissues, mutant myocilin is only associated with disease in the anterior segment of the eye, in the trabecular meshwork. The prevailing pathogenic mechanism involves a gain of toxic function whereby mutant myocilin aggregates intracellularly instead of being secreted, which causes cell stress and an early timeline for TM cell death, elevated intraocular pressure, and subsequent glaucoma-associated retinal degeneration. In this review, we focus on the work our lab has conducted over the past ∼15 years to enhance our molecular understanding of myocilin-associated glaucoma, which includes details of the molecular structure and the nature of the aggregates formed by mutant myocilin. We conclude by discussing open questions, such as predicting phenotype from genotype alone, the elusive native function of myocilin, and translational directions enabled by our work.

records.title: The pre-Descemet's layer (Dua's layer, also known as the Dua-Fine layer and the pre-posterior limiting lamina layer): Discovery, characterisation, clinical and surgical applications, and the controversy.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: The pre-Descemet's layer (Dua's layer, also known as the Dua-Fine layer and the pre-posterior limiting lamina layer): Discovery, characterisation, clinical and surgical applications, and the controversy.
content.abstract: The pre-Descemet's layer/Dua's layer, also termed the Dua-Fine layer and the pre-posterior limiting lamina layer, lies anterior to the Descemet's membrane in the cornea, is 10 μm (range 6-16) thick, made predominantly of type I and some type VI collagen with abundant elastin, more than any other layer of the cornea. It has high tensile strength (bursting pressure up to 700 mm of Hg), is impervious to air and almost acellular. At the periphery it demonstrates fenestrations and ramifies to become the core of the trabecular meshwork, with implications for intraocular pressure and glaucoma. It has been demonstrated in some species of animals. The layer has assumed considerable importance in anterior and posterior lamellar corneal transplant surgery by improving our understanding of the behaviour of corneal tissue during these procedures, improved techniques and made the surgery safer with better outcomes. It has led to the innovation of new surgical procedures namely, pre-Descemet's endothelial keratoplasty, suture management of acute hydrops, DALK-triple and Fogla's mini DALK. The discovery and knowledge of the layer has introduced paradigm shifts in our age old concepts of Descemet's membrane detachment, acute corneal hydrops in keratoconus and Descemetoceles, with impact on management approaches. It has been shown to contribute to the pathology and clinical signs observed in corneal infections and some corneal dystrophies. Early evidence suggests that it may have a role in the pathogenesis of keratoconus in relation to its elastin content. Its contribution to corneal biomechanics and glaucoma are subjects of current investigations.

records.title: The OCT angular sign of Henle fiber layer (HFL) hyperreflectivity (ASHH) and the pathoanatomy of the HFL in macular disease.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: The OCT angular sign of Henle fiber layer (HFL) hyperreflectivity (ASHH) and the pathoanatomy of the HFL in macular disease.
content.abstract: The Henle fiber layer (HFL) is comprised of bundles of unmyelinated photoreceptor axons intermingled with outer Müller cell processes. The photoreceptor axons extend from the cell bodies located in the outer nuclear layer and radially project toward the outer plexiform layer, the inner third of which includes the synaptic junctional complexes and the outer two-thirds of which includes the HFL. The oblique path of the HFL provides unique structural and reflectance properties and this radial anatomy is highlighted in many macular disorders including those with macular star exudation and HFL hemorrhage. Recent investigations using multimodal imaging techniques, especially cross sectional and en face optical coherence tomography (OCT), have provided new perspectives regarding HFL disruption in retinal diseases. The aim of this review is to highlight the pathoanatomy and multimodal imaging, especially OCT, associated with HFL disruption that is present in various macular diseases. After describing the current knowledge of the embryology, anatomy, and physiology of the HFL, we review the existing imaging modalities that allow in vivo visualization of the HFL in the healthy and diseased retina. Finally, we report the clinical and imaging findings of acute HFL alteration in various macular disorders, including degenerative, inflammatory, and vascular conditions. Also, we propose a novel and signature OCT biomarker indicative of acute photoreceptor disruption involving the HFL, termed the "angular sign of HFL hyperreflectivity" (ASHH) of macular disease, to unify the pathoanatomy common to these various macular disorders and to provide clarity regarding the underlying pathogenesis.

records.title: Design and Conduct of Randomized Clinical Trials Evaluating Surgical Innovations in Ophthalmology: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Design and Conduct of Randomized Clinical Trials Evaluating Surgical Innovations in Ophthalmology: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Surgical innovations are necessary to improve patient care. After an initial exploratory phase, novel surgical technique should be compared with alternative options or standard care in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). However, surgical RCTs have unique methodological challenges. Our study sought to investigate key aspects of the design, conduct, and reporting of RCTs of novel surgeries.

Design

Systematic review.

Methods

The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021253297). RCTs evaluating novel surgeries for cataract, vitreoretinal, glaucoma, and corneal diseases were included. Medline, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and Clinicaltrials.gov were searched. The search period was January 1, 2016, to June 16, 2021.

Results

A total of 52 ophthalmic surgery RCTs were identified in the fields of glaucoma (n = 12), vitreoretinal surgery (n = 5), cataract (n = 19), and cornea (n = 16). A description defining the surgeon's experience or level of expertise was reported in 30 RCTs (57%) and was presented in both control and intervention groups in 11 (21%). Specification of the number of cases performed in the particular surgical innovation being assessed prior to the trial was reported in 10 RCTs (19%) and an evaluation of quality of the surgical intervention in 7 (13%). Prospective trial registration was recorded in 12 RCTs (23%) and retrospective registration in 13 (25%); and there was no registration record in the remaining 28 (53%) studies.

Conclusions

Important aspects of the study design such as the surgical learning curve, surgeon's previous experience, quality assurance, and trial registration details were often missing in novel ophthalmic surgical procedures. The Idea, Development, Exploration, Assessment, Long-term follow-up (IDEAL) framework aims to improve the quality of study design.

records.title: Activation of retinal glial cells contributes to the degeneration of ganglion cells in experimental glaucoma.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Activation of retinal glial cells contributes to the degeneration of ganglion cells in experimental glaucoma.
content.abstract: Elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP) is a major risk factor for neurodegeneration in glaucoma. Glial cells, which play an important role in normal functioning of retinal neurons, are well involved into retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration in experimental glaucoma animal models generated by elevated IOP. In response to elevated IOP, mGluR I is first activated and Kir4.1 channels are subsequently inhibited, which leads to the activation of Müller cells. Müller cell activation is followed by a complex process, including proliferation, release of inflammatory and growth factors (gliosis). Gliosis is further regulated by several factors. Activated Müller cells contribute to RGC degeneration through generating glutamate receptor-mediated excitotoxicity, releasing cytotoxic factors and inducing microglia activation. Elevated IOP activates microglia, and following morphological and functional changes, these cells, as resident immune cells in the retina, show adaptive immune responses, including an enhanced release of pro-inflammatory factors (tumor neurosis factor-α, interleukins, etc.). These ATP and Toll-like receptor-mediated responses are further regulated by heat shock proteins, CD200R, chemokine receptors, and metabotropic purinergic receptors, may aggravate RGC loss. In the optic nerve head, astrogliosis is initiated and regulated by a complex reaction process, including purines, transmitters, chemokines, growth factors and cytokines, which contributes to RGC axon injury through releasing pro-inflammatory factors and changing extracellular matrix in glaucoma. The effects of activated glial cells on RGCs are further modified by the interplay among different types of glial cells. This review is concluded by presenting an in-depth discussion of possible research directions in this field in the future.

records.title: Advances in understanding the molecular structure of retinoschisin while questions remain of biological function.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Advances in understanding the molecular structure of retinoschisin while questions remain of biological function.
content.abstract: Retinoschisin (RS1) is a secreted protein that is essential for maintaining integrity of the retina. Numerous mutations in RS1 cause X-linked retinoschisis (XLRS), a progressive degeneration of the retina that leads to vision loss in young males. A key manifestation of XLRS is the formation of cavities (cysts) in the retina and separation of the layers (schisis), disrupting synaptic transmission. There are currently no approved treatments for patients with XLRS. Strategies using adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors to deliver functional copies of RS1 as a form of gene augmentation therapy, are under clinical evaluation. To improve therapeutic strategies for treating XLRS, it is critical to better understand the secretion of RS1 and its molecular function. Immunofluorescence and immunoelectron microscopy show that RS1 is located on the surfaces of the photoreceptor inner segments and bipolar cells. Sequence homology indicates a discoidin domain fold, similar to many other proteins with demonstrated adhesion functions. Recent structural studies revealed the tertiary structure of RS1 as two back-to-back octameric rings, each cross-linked by disulfides. The observation of higher order structures in vitro suggests the formation of an adhesive matrix spanning the distance between cells (∼100 nm). Several studies indicated that RS1 readily binds to other proteins such as the sodium-potassium ATPase (NaK-ATPase) and extracellular matrix proteins. Alternatively, RS1 may influence fluid regulation via interaction with membrane proteins such as the NaK-ATPase, largely inferred from the use of carbonic anhydrase inhibitors to shrink the typical intra-retinal cysts in XLRS. We discuss these models in light of RS1 structure and address the difficulty in understanding the function of RS1.

records.title: Genome-wide Survival Analysis for Macular Neovascularization Development in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy Revealed Shared Genetic Susceptibility with Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy.

content.title: Genome-wide Survival Analysis for Macular Neovascularization Development in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy Revealed Shared Genetic Susceptibility with Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To identify susceptibility genes for macular neovascularization (MNV) development in central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC).

Design

Genome-wide survival analysis using a longitudinal cohort study.

Participants

We included 402 and 137 patients with CSC but without MNV at their first visit from the Kyoto CSC Cohort and Kobe CSC dataset, respectively. All patients underwent detailed ophthalmic examinations, including multimodal imaging, such as fundus autofluorescence, spectral-domain OCT, and fluorescein angiography/indocyanine green angiography or OCT angiography.

Methods

We conducted a genome-wide survival analysis using the Kyoto CSC Cohort. We applied the Cox proportional hazard model to adjust for age, sex, and the first principal component. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with P values < 1.0 × 10-5 were carried forward to the replication in the Kobe CSC dataset. Moreover, we evaluated the contribution of previously reported age-related macular degeneration (AMD) susceptibility loci. We used FUMA and ToppFun for the functional enrichment analysis.

Main outcome measures

The association between SNPs and MNV development in patients with CSC.

Results

Rs370974631 near ARMS2 displayed a genome-wide significant association in the meta-analysis of discovery and replication result (hazard ratio [HR]meta, 3.63; Pmeta = 5.76 × 10-9). Among previously reported AMD susceptibility loci, we additionally identified CFH rs800292 (HR, 0.39, P = 2.55 × 10-4), COL4A3 rs4276018 (HR, 0.26, P = 1.56 × 10-3), and B3GALTL rs9564692 (HR, 0.56, P = 8.30 × 10-3) as susceptibility loci for MNV development in CSC. The functional enrichment analysis revealed significant enrichment of 8 pathways (GO:0051561, GO:0036444, GO:0008282, GO:1990246, GO:0015272, GO:0030955, GO:0031420, and GO:0005242) related to ion transport.

Conclusions

ARMS2, CFH, COL4A3, and B3GALTL were identified as susceptibility genes for MNV development in CSC. These 4 genes are known as susceptibility genes for AMD, whereas COL4A3 and B3GALTL were previously reported to be polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV)-specific susceptibility genes. Our findings revealed the shared genetic susceptibility between PCV and MNV secondary to CSC.

records.title: Exploring the contribution of ARMS2 and HTRA1 genetic risk factors in age-related macular degeneration.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Exploring the contribution of ARMS2 and HTRA1 genetic risk factors in age-related macular degeneration.
content.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of severe irreversible central vision loss in individuals over 65 years old. Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have shown that the region at chromosome 10q26, where the age-related maculopathy susceptibility (ARMS2/LOC387715) and HtrA serine peptidase 1 (HTRA1) genes are located, represents one of the strongest associated loci for AMD. However, the underlying biological mechanism of this genetic association has remained elusive. In this article, we extensively review the literature by us and others regarding the ARMS2/HTRA1 risk alleles and their functional significance. We also review the literature regarding the presumed function of the ARMS2 protein and the molecular processes of the HTRA1 protein in AMD pathogenesis in vitro and in vivo, including those of transgenic mice overexpressing HtrA1/HTRA1 which developed Bruch's membrane (BM) damage, choroidal neovascularization (CNV), and polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV), similar to human AMD patients. The elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of the ARMS2 and HTRA1 susceptibility loci has begun to untangle the complex biological pathways underlying AMD pathophysiology, pointing to new testable paradigms for treatment.

records.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Automated Macular Hole Diagnosis and Structured Report Generation.

content.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Automated Macular Hole Diagnosis and Structured Report Generation.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Current AI models for optical coherence tomography (OCT) primarily focus on diagnosis as a standalone task. We developed and validated an end-to-end agentic AI workflow that integrates automated macular hole (MH) diagnosis from OCT images with structured patient-friendly report generation.

Methods

The proposed sequential workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent consisted of an image diagnosis stage and a language generation step. The OCT version of RETFound, a self-supervised retinal foundation model, was fine-tuned for binary classification of macular OCT scans as MH or normal macula. Training, validation, and internal testing were performed using multiple public OCT datasets with patient-level stratified splitting, followed by external validation on two independent datasets. The performance of the fine-tuned foundation model was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC). For each new OCT image, the AI agent used the trained RETFound model to classify the image, received the diagnostic output, incorporated it into a structured prompt, and called the large language model (GPT-4) to generate the clinical report.

Results

On the internal test set (n = 180), the model achieved an accuracy of 100% (95% confidence interval (CI), 97.9-100%) with an AUC of 1.00. On external validation (n = 1014), accuracy was 98.8% (95% CI 97.9-99.3%), sensitivity was 97.9% (95% CI 96.3-98.8%), specificity was 100% (95% CI 99.2-100.0%), and AUC was 0.999 (95% CI 0.998-1.000). Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis showed that predictions were driven by relevant retinal regions, particularly the macular hole and adjacent layers. The end-to-end agentic AI workflow generated concise and standardized patient-friendly reports for all samples, without the language model influencing diagnostic decisions.

Conclusions

This study demonstrates the feasibility of an end-to-end AI workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent for robust OCT-based MH diagnosis with a large language model for structured report generation. By separating image-based diagnosis from language generation, this approach offers a practical and scalable solution for virtual vitreoretinal clinics.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Laser-Assisted Refractive Surgery-A Comprehensive Review.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Laser-Assisted Refractive Surgery-A Comprehensive Review.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology-in the form of Machine Learning (ML) models and other models specialized in image recognition and processing, such as Convolutional Neural Networks Visual Transformers (CNN-ViTs)-is increasingly being used in ophthalmology. This review summarizes the main AI applications for laser-assisted refractive surgery. Methods: A wide-ranging literature search on the PubMed and ISI Thompson Web of Science databases was conducted. Results: AI is an all-encompassing technological concept that refers to either specific applications of ML/CNN models, such as in keratoconus screening or diagnosis, or agentic/multimodal AI applications that process different data types using a variety of AI models. The most clinically established applications found were corneal ectasia and keratoconus screening, in which AI models can reliably exceed 95% diagnostic accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity; nomogram-derived laser ablation programming; optimization of ray-tracing calculations for ray-traced ablation profiles; patient screening and selection for refractive surgery; visual and refractive result prediction; assessment of postoperative corneal ectasia risk; detection of intraoperative complications; research on the laser coupling effect; and other applications such as monitoring eye rubbing behavior in corneal ectasia suspects. Thus, singular, specific applications of AI models have made the largest clinical contributions. These results must be interpreted with a comparison of internal versus external validation, calibration, and generalizability. Overall the technology is highly promising. Agentic/multimodal AI frameworks are currently being discussed, with pilot studies published and applicability proposed in the context of large, high-patient-volume clinical practices. The technological advent of SHAP force plot graphs and saliency maps has improved understanding of the factors that contribute mechanistically to AI model reasoning, leading to more informed clinical decisions or research applicability, such as in finding parameters or factors linked to postoperative ectasia. Conclusions: AI is already established in laser-assisted refractive surgery in the form of models specialized in data-intensive analysis. At present, the best-performing novel AI models originate from the domain of large or multi-hospital settings due to requirements for multiple latest-generation diagnostic devices, high-volume patient data, computing expertise, and resources. Future directions could include clinical standardization and trickle-down dissemination of the technology. Agentic/multimodal AI has the potential to benefit large clinical/patient settings or offer access to expert knowledge in smaller practice settings. Agentic/multimodal AI implementation is offset by challenges in complexity, the technological limitations of LLMs ("hallucinations"), and ethical and legislative factors.

records.title: Smartphone-Based Deep Learning Exophthalmometry in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Multicenter, Multiethnic Validation Study.
records.publisher: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association

content.title: Smartphone-Based Deep Learning Exophthalmometry in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Multicenter, Multiethnic Validation Study.
content.abstract:
Background

Proptosis is the principal quantitative measure of disease severity in thyroid eye disease (TED), but Hertel exophthalmometry has substantial interobserver variability and requires in-person specialist visits. Existing deep learning (DL) proptosis-from-photograph models require studio-acquired images. We aimed to validate, in a multicenter multiethnic study, a DL model fine-tuned to estimate proptosis (mm) from nonstudio facial photographs-smartphone selfies or clinician-taken photographs.

Methods

This validation study included 361 patients with confirmed or suspected TED at three institutions. Data were collected prospectively at two Korean sites-Severance Hospital (SH; 203 patients/3654 facial images; internal validation) and Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH; 79/933; same-ethnicity external validation)-and retrospectively, from routine-care images, at one Spanish site, Virgen Macarena University Hospital (HUVM; 79/336; different-ethnicity external validation). Korean patients self-acquired selfies on six smartphone models per site using a capture-guidance application; Spanish images were clinician-acquired during routine care without such guidance. The model-a dual-stream ResNet-18 jointly processing a facial image and a per-pixel depth map (ZoeDepth)-outputs a proptosis estimate (mm) per eye from one photograph and was fine-tuned, from a previously published model trained on studio digital single-lens reflex photographs, for these nonstudio acquisitions. Hertel measurements by oculoplastic specialists served as the reference standard.

Results

On single-image analysis, the mean absolute error (MAE) versus Hertel measurement was 1.14 mm (Pearson correlation coefficient [PCC] 0.83) in SH, 1.44 mm (PCC 0.85) in SNUBH, and 1.58 mm (PCC 0.77) in HUVM, with predictions within 2 mm of Hertel in 83.6%, 71.3%, and 69.7% of images, respectively. Performance was consistent across 12 smartphone models (per-device MAE 1.11-1.54 mm). For detecting severe proptosis (Hertel ≥21 mm), the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.94 (confidence interval 0.93-0.96), 0.91 (0.89-0.92), and 0.86 (0.82-0.91) in SH, SNUBH, and HUVM, respectively. Bland-Altman analysis revealed underestimation at the upper extreme.

Conclusions

An artificial intelligence model fine-tuned for nonstudio facial photographs achieved Hertel-level agreement and reliable severity discrimination across 2 ethnicities and 12 smartphones, both for patient self-acquired smartphone selfies and for clinician-acquired routine clinic photographs, providing a scalable approach for patient-facing and clinic-based monitoring of TED severity, pending further longitudinal validation.

records.title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.

content.title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.
content.abstract:
Aims

Whether a retinal artificial intelligence (AI) risk score reclassifies SCORE2 cardiovascular risk stratification in statin-naive adults across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary is uncertain. We evaluated the retinal AI risk score for 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prediction.

Methods

In 40,672 statin-naive UK Biobank participants (aged 40-69, without diabetes), cardiovascular risk categories and treatment recommendation status (Class I or IIa vs neither) were defined using the 2025 ESC/EAS focused-update framework. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) adjusted for SCORE2 or for established risk factors. The incremental predictive value of adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation.

Results

Over a 10.0-year median follow-up (914 ASCVD events), the very high retinal AI risk group independently predicted ASCVD (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.32 vs low risk; p<0.001). Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 reclassified risk across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary (statin-eligibility NRI [net reclassification improvement] 0.012, p<0.001); reclassification was statistically significant but modest (continuous NRI 0.445, p<0.001), without C-index or net-benefit gain. In the statin-indicated subgroup, retinal AI risk groups further stratified risk (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.16; p<0.001). Statin-not-indicated participants in the high or very high retinal AI risk groups had numerically similar observed 10-year risk to all statin-indicated, untreated participants (p=0.758). There was no evidence of effect modification by clinically detectable retinal disorder (interaction p=0.93). Incremental value was greater in women than men (sex interaction p<0.001).

Conclusion

Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 produced modest bidirectional risk reclassification across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary; these findings warrant prospective validation.Abstract word count: 250 words.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mass Spectrometry-Based Metabolomics and Lipidomics for Drug Discovery and Development.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mass Spectrometry-Based Metabolomics and Lipidomics for Drug Discovery and Development.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence applied to mass spectrometry-based metabolomics and lipidomics has advanced through three technological generations: chemometric and classical machine learning, deep learning, and self-supervised foundation models, with large language models so far entering mainly at the edges. The metabolome and lipidome lie closest to drug action, yet they have been among the slowest omics layers to adopt modern artificial intelligence. This paradox arises from their downstream position, which leaves them without a closed molecular reference and without the standardized, readily modeled data available to the genome and transcriptome. This review examines what these methods contribute to drug discovery and development. We survey applications across the drug-development pipeline, from target identification and mechanism of action deconvolution, through the prediction of drug-induced toxicity, to pharmacometabolomics, in which pre-dose metabolic phenotypes inform patient stratification and dosing. Across these metabolomic and lipidomic applications, interpretable classical machine learning remains the dominant form of artificial intelligence. The newer deep-learning and foundation models have concentrated instead on compound annotation, the cross-cutting problem of assigning confident identities to spectra, yet successive generations have mitigated but not solved it. Beyond annotation confidence, batch effects, semi-quantification, and small-cohort overfitting also remain practical constraints. Overall, targeted, hypothesis-driven metabolomic and lipidomic studies can already support drug discovery when their inferences are restricted to confidently identified metabolites, whereas open, hypothesis-free discovery remains the frontier. Near-term progress will depend less on any single algorithm than on curated spectral resources, rigorous measurement, leakage-aware validation, and honest reporting of identification confidence.

records.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.

content.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.
content.abstract:
Rationale and objectives

To evaluate the feasibility of a quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-to-structured reporting pipeline that integrates quantitative MRI software with large language models (LLMs) for structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers and generating clinician-facing report conclusions.

Materials and methods

A total of 192 patients with 3D T1 and 2D or 3D FLAIR MRI images from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database were randomly selected. A deep-learning model generated structured report findings based on nine indices related to brain atrophy, white matter hyperintensities, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space abnormalities, and compared with neuroradiologist-generated reference reports. Four LLMs (GPT-OSS 20B, MedGemma 4B, Phi-3, and Llama 3.1 8B) generated clinician-facing conclusions from the structured findings. Generated conclusions were evaluated using a five-point Likert scale across four metrics (accuracy, relevance, clarity, and satisfaction). Output errors were assessed across four categories: language, omission, addition, and numeric errors.

Results

Structured report findings demonstrated high accuracy for CSF space analysis (77.6%-97.9%). Performance for ordinal visual scales was lower under strict matching (27.1%-57.8%) but improved with a one-grade tolerance (91.7%-97.4%). Among LLMs, GPT achieved the highest scores across most metrics (median score 5) and exhibited the lowest output error rates. Smaller models (Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B) showed overall lower performance, with more language, omission, and addition errors. MedGemma demonstrated intermediate performance, but the highest rate of numeric errors.

Conclusion

Our quantitative MRI-to-structured reporting pipeline, integrating quantitative MRI software with LLM-based conclusion generation, might be feasible for automated structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers.

records.title: Histopathological Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for Cancer Diagnosis and Gleason Grading: A Brief Review of Prostate Cancer.
records.publisher: Journal of clinical practice and research

content.title: Histopathological Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for Cancer Diagnosis and Gleason Grading: A Brief Review of Prostate Cancer.
content.abstract:
Objective

Prostate cancer, one of the most common cancers affecting men's health worldwide, ranks second among cancer-related deaths. Therefore, it represents a critical health issue, and early diagnosis is crucial. Several imaging and analytical methods are used to diagnose this condition.

Materials and methods

This study focuses on research conducted between 2021 and 2025 that analyzes, diagnoses, and grades prostate cancer based on histopathological images using machine learning and deep learning algorithms. In this context, the reviewed studies also include an analysis of findings related to preprocessing and feature extraction methods that may aid in prostate cancer detection, as well as the classifiers used.

Results

According to the findings of the reviewed studies, artificial intelligence-supported prostate cancer detection systems demonstrate high clinical performance and significantly improve the diagnostic accuracy of pathologists by enabling rapid diagnosis. The presented research findings indicate a need for comprehensive studies focusing on prostate cancer using histopathological images.

Conclusion

The integration of artificial intelligence is transforming prostate cancer pathology from a traditional and subjective process into a data-driven and standardized framework. This systematic analysis of histopathological images will make significant contributions to future prostate cancer research, help achieve more reliable results in clinical decision-making processes, and lay the groundwork for personalized medicine.

records.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics.

content.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been significantly improved through deep learning techniques; however, the lack of interpretability remains a major challenge for clinical adoption. Methods: This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-driven framework for multiclass brain tumor classification using a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) and four transfer learning models, namely ResNet50, DenseNet121, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNetB0. The models were trained and evaluated on a publicly available brain MRI dataset consisting of glioma, meningioma, and pituitary tumor classes. Their classification performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), and confusion matrix analysis. To enhance transparency and interpretability, Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP were used to visualize and quantify the regions contributing to the classification decisions. Results: Experimental results state that the transfer learning models consistently outperformed the CNN by learning more discriminative feature representations while producing more localized and interpretable explanations. The agreement among Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP confirms that the proposed models predominantly relied on tumor regions rather than irrelevant background information, thereby improving the interpretability and reliability of the diagnostic predictions. Conclusions: The proposed framework provides an effective and explainable computer-aided diagnosis system that supports trustworthy deep learning-based brain tumor classification and has the potential for decision-making.

records.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study.

content.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study.
content.abstract:
Background

Spirometry is one of the most used pulmonary function tests for assessing respiratory function and diagnosing ventilatory disorders in clinical practice. Evaluation of test validity and interpretation is typically performed by trained healthcare professionals. The present study aims to evaluate the capability of a publicly available large language model (LLM) to perform quality assurance and interpretations of spirometry tests.

Methods

A total of 150 spirometry tests were retrospectively collected from the pulmonary function laboratories. The spirometry tests were evaluated for acceptability and interpreted by clinicians according to ATS/ERS recommendations as part of standard clinical practice. Subsequently, a publicly available LLM (ChatGPT 5.5) was prompted to evaluate the acceptability and interpret the same spirometry tests according to ATS/ERS criteria. The model interpreted each spirometry test on three separate occasions for assessing reproducibility. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were calculated by comparing LLM assessments with clinician assessments of spirometry test acceptability and interpretation.

Results

For spirometry acceptability evaluation, ChatGPT demonstrated an overall accuracy of 87% (95% CI: 81%-92%), sensitivity of 91% (95% CI: 85%-95%), specificity of 61% (95% CI 39%-80%), PPV of 94% (95% CI: 89%-97%), and NPV of 48(95% CI: 29%-67%) with Cohen's k of 0.46. The spiromteric interpretation agreement with the clinicians reference standard was moderate, with exact agreement of 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54-0.69) while Cohen's Kappa (Unweighted) was 0.47 (95% CI: 0.37-0.56) and Macro F1 score was 0.39 (95% CI: 0.33-0.49). Reproducibility across three independent trials was moderate (Fleiss' κ 0.58). Class-specific interpretation performance varied by category; sensitivity was highest for normal pattern and restrictive defects (0.72), whereas sensitivity for obstructive defects was 0.27. F1-scores were highest for normal and restrictive defects (0.81 and 0.62, respectively).

Conclusion

The current findings suggest that ChatGPT 5.5 has a limited capability, at its current stage of development, to serve as a reliable tool for independent spirometry interpretation in clinical practice. Nevertheless, it may serve as an adjunct to clinical decision-making and educational tools. Prospective controlled studies are needed to confirm these findings.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
content.abstract:
Background

Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously.

Objectives

To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer.

Methods

PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines.

Results

Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry.

Conclusions

Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

records.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.

content.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), especially the recent proliferation of generative Large Language Models (LLMs), is transforming traditional anatomy education by introducing new teaching tools. However, the adoption of these cutting-edge technologies raises questions about global educational equity. It remains unclear whether AI will serve as a digital equalizer or further exacerbate marginalization. This rapid bibliometric synthesis aims to provide a comprehensive, data-driven overview of the "Application of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education" (AAAE). We seek to map the intellectual landscape, detect structural and technological shifts, evaluate the geopolitical disparities, and provide corresponding references. A total of 85 consolidated records were retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. These data constituted the whole panorama of AAAE. Bibliometrix and CiteSpace were utilized for static and dynamic mapping. A multidisciplinary expert panel validated the thematic clusters using Gwet's AC1 and the Normalized Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI). Publications surged following ChatGPT's release, indicating a shift from specialized computer vision to the application of general-purpose LLMs. While high-income countries maintain leadership, AI could exert a "democratizing effect" on upper-middle-income countries, doubling their odds of publication compared to traditional anatomy. Six research frontiers and three research trajectories were captured, and corresponding implications for future researchers in the global south and north were presented. AAAE could be conducted using a stratified strategy: different expansions of AI technologies for pedagogy; leveraging commercial APIs to bypass infrastructure bottlenecks; and validating open-source models. Global equity critically demands cross-border collaboration and inclusive datasets.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning Approaches for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis: Protocol for a Scoping Review.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning Approaches for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis: Protocol for a Scoping Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects over 366 million adults and 139 million children worldwide, yet diagnosis remains fundamentally subjective, relying on clinical interviews, behavioral observations, and rating scales that yield inconsistent results across practitioners and settings. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) offer a paradigm shift toward objective, data-driven diagnosis by detecting complex patterns across neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and digital biomarkers that elude conventional assessment. Although AI-based ADHD research has grown exponentially, no comprehensive synthesis examines the full spectrum of data modalities, validation practices, and clinical translation readiness. This gap limits our understanding of which approaches are most promising for real-world implementation.

Objective

This scoping review will visually map the current evidence on AI-based ADHD classification with respect to predictive accuracy, data forms, data features, generalizability, and interpretability of models.

Methods

This scoping review will use the Joanna Briggs Institute approach to scoping reviews and follow the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Five electronic databases (IEEE Xplore, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and ACM Digital Library) will be systematically searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2019 and April 2026. Empirical studies in English involving the use of AI, ML, DL, or explainable AI to diagnose ADHD with a total sample size greater than 100 participants (ADHD and control groups combined) and a non-ADHD control group (individuals with typical development or healthy individuals) will be included. Two independent reviewers will screen the titles, abstracts, and full texts, and any conflicts will be resolved through either discussion or arbitration. A standardized Microsoft Excel template will be used to extract data that will include the following: bibliographic data, data modalities, data models, data validation approaches, performance metrics, and explainability approaches. Thematic and narrative analysis will be used to synthesize findings on 4 research questions that will address model performance, data modality contributions, data characteristics, and interpretability methods.

Results

The scoping review began in December 2025. Analysis and screening are in progress, with the scoping review expected to be completed and submitted for publication in June 2026.

Conclusions

This scoping review will provide the first comprehensive synthesis of AI-, ML-, and DL-based ADHD diagnostic classification studies, mapping the evidence across data modalities, validation practices, interpretability methods, and clinical translation readiness. Findings will inform future methodological standards and support the translation of AI-based diagnostic tools into clinical practice.

records.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Chatbots in University Level Dental Education: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Chatbots in University Level Dental Education: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI), mainly AI-driven chatbots and large language models (LLMs) is reshaping dental education through adaptive, interactive, and simulation-based learning. While the transition in technology has been rapid, the evidence about the educational effectiveness of these technologies is still very diverse and not entirely directed.

Aim

To analyze the roles, educational effectiveness, and impact of integrating AI-driven chatbots and LLMs in dental education at the university level with a focus on learning outcomes and implementation practices.

Methods

The researchers conducted a thorough search of the electronic databases PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase for articles published from January 2018 to November 2025. This review met the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 criteria and was made up of original research articles on dental studentsand educators who were using AI-based chatbots as interventions. The outcomes measured were knowledge gain, clinical reasoning, diagnostic accuracy, communication skills, and engagement of learners. Due to the differences in the methodologies used the authors opted for a narrative synthesis approach.

Results

Six studies met the eligibility criteria and showed potential benefits of AI-driven chatbots and LLMs for diagnostic reasoning, learning performance, engagement, and individualized feedback although methodological and outcome heterogeneity limited direct comparison.

Conclusion

AI-driven chatbots and LLMs may complement university-level dental education, but their effectiveness and safe implementation require further rigorous evaluation.

records.title: The Influence of Large Language Model-Generated Artificial Intelligence Risk Estimates on Clinical Decision-Making in Breast Imaging: A Simulation-Based Study.

content.title: The Influence of Large Language Model-Generated Artificial Intelligence Risk Estimates on Clinical Decision-Making in Breast Imaging: A Simulation-Based Study.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision-support tools in radiology, yet their influence on clinical decision-making remains a significant concern. This study evaluates how artificial intelligence (AI)-generated malignancy risk estimates influence clinical decisions in breast imaging and assesses automation bias (AB) among radiology residents at different training levels. Methods: In this simulation-based study, 20 residents reviewed radiology reports for 15 synthetic breast imaging cases generated by ChatGPT-4 Turbo, each presented in either a concordant or discordant format. Participants were stratified into two groups based on their completion of a breast imaging rotation and evaluated each case by assigning a BI-RADS score, recommending management, and rating their confidence in the AI risk estimate. Diagnostic accuracy and independent predictors of AB were analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) to account for reader-level clustering. Results: Overall management accuracy was significantly lower in cases with discordant AI outputs (p = 0.008). A similar, albeit non-significant, decreasing trend was observed for BI-RADS accuracy. While advanced residents maintained high management accuracy regardless of AI concordance, early-stage residents showed a sharp decline in discordant cases (77.3% vs. 45.3%; p = 0.006). This decline was most critical in malignant cases for early-stage residents, where accuracy dropped from 92.0% to 48.0% (p < 0.001). In the multivariable GEE logistic regression model, training level was the only independent predictor of AB (OR: 0.09, 95% CI: 0.03-0.28, p < 0.001). Conclusions: In this simulation study, advanced clinical training was associated with lower susceptibility to AB in breast imaging, although training level alone is unlikely to be a sufficient safeguard. Safe integration of AI tools will require caution among junior trainees alongside system-level measures such as model transparency and institutional oversight.

records.title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract: The rapid accumulation of multi-omics data provides increasing opportunities for cancer biomarker discovery, but the heterogeneity and high dimensionality of these datasets remain major challenges for data integration and analysis. This review examines the application of bioinformatics and artificial intelligence for multi-omics integration in cancer biomarker research. Common multi-omics data paradigms and integration strategies are discussed, followed by a review of the bioinformatics, machine learning and deep learning approaches applied across 84 included studies. Cross-study comparison showed limited recurrence among the reported biomarkers, with only 15 biomarkers identified in at least four studies. Further assessment of the 13 recurrent protein-coding biomarkers showed significant protein-protein interaction enrichment and functional convergence in cancer-related processes, particularly PI3K/AKT and ERBB2-related signaling. This review also highlights current challenges, including missing data, heterogeneity across datasets, limited independent validation and the interpretability of artificial intelligence models. Future research may benefit from integrating multi-omics data with clinical information, pathological imaging, electronic health records, single-cell multi-omics and radiomics, together with broader datasets and greater use of independent validation to support the translation of multi-omics biomarker findings into clinical applications.

records.title: Comparative analysis and optimization of multi-model artificial intelligence for microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections.
records.publisher: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

content.title: Comparative analysis and optimization of multi-model artificial intelligence for microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections.
content.abstract:
Background

Superficial fungal infections present a growing threat to global public health. Traditional diagnostic techniques, including microscopy and culture, are time-consuming and subjective, often limiting diagnostic accuracy. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven diagnostic tools offer a promising adjunct to improve efficiency and standardization of microscopic fungal detection.

Methods

We systematically compared six deep learning models, including the You Only Look Once (YOLO) series, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) series and the Detection Transformer (DETR). Three evaluation datasets were constructed. Datasets 1 and 2 (derived from 4000 hyphae and 4500 spore images) were used to assess image-level detection using sensitivity, precision and F1 score. Dataset 1 was manually annotated for the YOLO series and DETR; Dataset 2 (unannotated) served as the CNN series' benchmark. Dataset 3 (1, 870 specimens from 1, 730 patients) was used to evaluate sample-level performance via confusion matrix analysis for the YOLO series and DETR models, employing medical records as the reference standard. The best-performing model was optimized and deployed into an online auxiliary diagnostic platform for real-time clinical decision support.

Results

YOLOv11 outperformed all other evaluated architectures. Detection was generally better at 400× than at 200× magnification. Notably, the F1 score for hyphae detection by YOLOv11 increased from 90.42% (200×) to 92.06% (400×). All models achieved higher accuracy for spores than hyphae. Patient-level confusion-matrix analysis confirmed YOLOv11 superiority. After optimizing an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.25 and the maximum confidence (Cmax) strategy, 200× hyphae F1 rose to 97.84% and the positive predictive value (PPV) to 98.27%. Subgroup analysis showed robust performance across different diseases, with tinea capitis reaching the highest F1 score (98.53%).

Conclusion

The optimized YOLOv11 model demonstrates potential as a rapid and standardized supportive tool for the microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections. Integration into an online auxiliary diagnostic platform demonstrates the feasibility of real-time AI-assisted fungal detection, offering a standardized tool to support clinical decision-making. This work supports AI as a potential complement to clinical and laboratory expertise, pending further validation in prospective and multi-center settings, and highlights its potential to streamline fungal infection diagnostic workflows.

records.title: Effects of Curcumin Supplementation on Inflammatory Biomarkers in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

content.title: Effects of Curcumin Supplementation on Inflammatory Biomarkers in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Chronic low-grade inflammation contributes to the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated randomized evidence on the effects of oral curcumin or curcuminoid supplementation on circulating inflammatory biomarkers in adults with T2DM. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception through 31 August 2026. Random-effects models using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals were applied to the primary syntheses because relatively few studies contributed to each outcome. Results: Six randomized controlled trials (RCTs; n = 472) provided compatible hs-CRP endpoint data. Curcumin supplementation was associated with lower hs-CRP concentrations (MD = -1.06 mg/L; 95% CI -1.97 to -0.16; p = 0.030; I2 = 17.3%), although sensitivity analyses involving unit-ambiguous or statistically reconstructed data increased uncertainty. Five RCTs (n = 475) contributed quantitative TNF-α data; the pooled standardized effect favored curcumin (Hedges' g = -1.20; 95% CI -1.98 to -0.42; p = 0.013), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 84.9%). Evidence for IL-6 from three randomized cohorts was directionally favorable but heterogeneous and was synthesized narratively, whereas IL-1β findings were limited to a single randomized cohort. Conclusions: Curcumin or curcuminoid supplementation may reduce hs-CRP and TNF-α in adults with T2DM; however, the strength of inference is limited by the small evidence base, heterogeneity, and inconsistencies in outcome reporting. Larger, methodologically standardized trials are warranted.

records.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the association between low socioeconomic status and all-cause mortality in patients with diabetes.

content.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the association between low socioeconomic status and all-cause mortality in patients with diabetes.
content.abstract:
Objective

The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between socioeconomic status (SES) and all-cause mortality among individuals with diabetes. We also examined how individual SES components, including income, employment, education, and housing conditions, were associated with mortality risk.

Methods

Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science through September 2025. Eligible studies included adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes reporting associations between SES indicators (income, education, occupation, or area-level deprivation) and all-cause mortality. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using fixed- or random-effects models based on heterogeneity (I2). Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger's test.

Results

Nineteen studies were included. Low SES was associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality (OR = 1.67; 95% CI: 1.49-1.88; p < 0.00001). Similar associations were observed across income, education, housing, and employment domains. Heterogeneity was substantial (I 2 = 99%), indicating considerable variability across studies. Sensitivity analyses showed that no single study materially influenced the pooled estimate, and publication bias appeared minimal.

Conclusion

Low socioeconomic status is associated with increased mortality among individuals with diabetes. Addressing socioeconomic inequalities through improved access to education, employment opportunities, healthy environments, and equitable healthcare may help reduce survival disparities and mitigate the overall burden of diabetes.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?RecordID=1248984, identifier PROSPERO (CRD420251248984).

records.title: AI-Assisted Clinical Decision Support Versus Standard Teleconsultation in Adult Medicine: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Accuracy, Referral and Testing Decisions, and Clinician Confidence.

content.title: AI-Assisted Clinical Decision Support Versus Standard Teleconsultation in Adult Medicine: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Accuracy, Referral and Testing Decisions, and Clinician Confidence.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into teleconsultation, but its effects on clinician performance remain uncertain. We assessed whether clinician-facing AI improves diagnostic accuracy, reduces referrals or testing, and increases clinician confidence compared with standard teleconsultation or conventional resources. Methods: This retrospectively registered systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 and Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis (SWiM) guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE, publisher-indexed platforms, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov, and backward and forward citation searches were performed from inception to 1 August 2026. Eligible studies evaluated clinician-facing AI in adult primary, urgent, or general medical teleconsultation or in high-fidelity virtual consultation designs and reported diagnostic, referral/testing, or confidence outcomes. One reviewer screened records, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias using the design-appropriate QUADAS-2, RoB 2, and ROBINS-I domains, with a second pass for consistency. Owing to clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the results were synthesized narratively. Results: Of 31 records identified, 25 remained after duplicate removal, 18 full texts were assessed, and six studies were included: two randomized virtual experiments, two retrospectives virtual care cohorts, one randomized crossover conversational AI study, and one provider-to-provider telemedicine case series. In a telehealth screening experiment, AI improved diagnostic prediction, but physicians given a large language model showed no significant benefit (adjusted difference, two percentage points; 95% CI, -4 to 8). Across 102,059 virtual encounters, an AI-generated differential included the clinician's final diagnosis in 84.2%, although the reference was not independent. AI-assisted urgent care recommendations were rated optimal more often than final physician recommendations (77.1% vs. 67.1%). AI did not reduce unnecessary referrals; one experiment found more confirmatory testing requests and lower trust than with a familiar clinical score. Certainty was low or very low for the principal clinical outcomes. Conclusions: AI may support teleconsultation decisions, but evidence that it reduces unnecessary referrals or meaningfully increases clinician confidence is insufficient. Pragmatic trials using independent patient-level reference standards are needed. Registration: This completed review was retrospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF); no protocol was published before study selection.

records.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Tricyclic Antidepressants, Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors, and Anticonvulsants for Diabetic Painful Neuropathy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Tricyclic Antidepressants, Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors, and Anticonvulsants for Diabetic Painful Neuropathy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract: Introduction: Diabetic painful neuropathy (DPN) is one of the most common and debilitating complications of diabetes, substantially impairing the quality of life of patients. In the absence of disease-modifying therapies, treatment remains focused on symptomatic pain control with non-opioid pharmacologic agents; however, comparative evidence guiding optimal medication selection remains limited.
